lesson.title: Collapsing a Sequence Into One Answer
lesson.summary: reduce repeatedly combines the elements of an iterable using a function, folding an entire sequence down into a single accumulated value.
lesson.body:
map produces a transformed sequence and filter produces a smaller sequence, but sometimes you do not want a sequence back at all, you want one number, one string, one combined result, computed from every element. That is what reduce does. Unlike map and filter, reduce is not a builtin in Python 3, it lives in the functools module, so you must import it before using it: from functools import reduce.

reduce(function, iterable) takes a function of two arguments, an accumulator and the next item, and applies it cumulatively across the iterable, carrying the running result forward each time.

from functools import reduce

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]
total = reduce(lambda acc, x: acc + x, numbers)
print(total)

Trace: with no starting value supplied, reduce uses the first element as the initial accumulator. acc starts as 1. Then acc becomes 1 + 2 = 3. Then acc becomes 3 + 3 = 6. Then acc becomes 6 + 4 = 10. There are no elements left, so reduce returns 10, and the program prints 10.

reduce also accepts an optional third argument, an explicit starting value, which is useful both for clarity and for handling an empty iterable safely:

product = reduce(lambda acc, x: acc * x, numbers, 1)
print(product)

Trace: acc starts at the supplied initial value, 1. Then acc becomes 1 * 1 = 1, then 1 * 2 = 2, then 2 * 3 = 6, then 6 * 4 = 24. reduce returns 24, matching what you would get from multiplying every element of numbers together starting from 1.

reduce is not limited to arithmetic. It can implement logic that Python already gives you as a builtin, which is a good way to see what it is really doing under the hood:

from functools import reduce

values = [3, 7, 2, 9, 4]
largest = reduce(lambda acc, x: acc if acc > x else x, values)
print(largest)

Trace: acc starts as the first element, 3. Comparing acc to the next value, 7: acc is not greater than x, so acc becomes 7. Comparing 7 to 2: acc is greater, acc stays 7. Comparing 7 to 9: acc is not greater, acc becomes 9. Comparing 9 to 4: acc is greater, acc stays 9. No values remain, so reduce returns 9, matching what Python's built in max(values) would give directly. This is essentially how max is implemented conceptually: keep a running best answer and update it only when a better candidate appears.

reduce is the most general of the three, since sum, max, min, and even map and filter behaviors can all be expressed as a reduce with the right combining function, but that generality comes at a cost to readability. Because the accumulation happens step by step inside the function rather than being visible in a loop body, reduce chains can be harder to read at a glance than an equivalent for loop with a running total variable. Common Python style guidance leans toward using reduce sparingly, reaching for a plain loop or a builtin like sum() when one already exists for the job, and saving reduce for genuinely custom combining logic.

All three of map, filter, and reduce share the same foundation from higher order functions: each one accepts a function as an argument and lets that function decide the actual per element behavior, while the higher order function itself handles the mechanics of walking through the iterable.
